newsitem.title: USA: Sierra and Physicians put merger on hold.
newsitem.headline: Sierra and Physicians put merger on hold.

text.p: The proposed merger between Sierra Health Services Inc. and Physicians Corp. of America was put on hold Thursday in advance of Physicians' pending fourth quarter earnings.
Las Vegas-based Sierra said extensive losses at Physicians' workers' compensation unit prompted it to reassess the terms of the deal.

Both companies said Thursday the merger, which would have created the eighth largest publicly traded managed care company, will not proceed under the currently negotiated terms but they said the deal could still go ahead under new terms.

"Although we believe that there is value in PCA's core health maintenance organisation business, we want to protect Sierra from any recent and future adverse developments associated with PCA's workers' compensation division," Sierra Chairman Anthony Marlon said in a statement.
"If we decide to pursue a transaction, we will renegotiate the terms and announce them by March 31," he added.

On Nov. 4, Sierra agreed to merge with Miami-based Physicians in a deal which was valued at about $480 million. Sierra agreed to exchange 0.45 of its shares for each outstanding share of Physicians in a pooling of interests. The deal was slated to close on March 31.

On Feb. 21, Physicians said it would take a fourth quarter charge of $80 million related to increased liabilities at its workers' compensation unit. The charge was in addition to a similar charge of $130 million from November 1996.

"The charge that they announced regarding the fourth quarter was an adverse development that was not part of the original agreement and that was the impetus for us to reevaluate," said Ria Marie Carlson, a spokeswoman for Sierra.

"They haven't announced their earnings yet, they expect to do that next week. We need to wait for that announcement to come out," she said. "If we decide to pursue the transaction we will renegotiate the terms."
Michael Elwood, analyst at Volpe, Welty & Co., said Thursday's announcements came as no surprise.
"When they announced the fourth quarter charge we felt strongly that the deal could not get done, at least at the previously negotiated terms," he said.
Elwood said the exact size of Physicians' charge may be higher than the $80 million it has estimated.
"The amount of the loss has been somewhat ellusive ... it doesn't seem like (Physicians') actuaries have a real handle on the size of the problem," he said.
Nevertheless he expects Sierra will try and make the merger work if it can renegotiate the terms to shield it from the excessive losses at the workers' compensation unit.
